extracted.intended_audience: researchers, research-integrity officers, journal editors, science journalists, and the academic community interested in research misconduct cases
extracted.subtask_description: A blog-style report summarizing the Office of Research Integrity (ORI) findings about Marc Hauser, documenting specific instances of fabrication/falsification, misreporting of methods/results, and administrative sanctions. Useful as a case study of research misconduct types and consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fabrication of data in published figure
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent published fabricated data in Figure 2 of the paper Hauser, M.D., Weiss, D., & Marcus, G. 'Rule learning by cotton-top tamarins.' Cognition 86:B15-B22, 2002 — half of the data in the graph was fabricated; the reported bar heights and subject counts were false (e.g., reported proportions that equated to fractional subject counts like 7.14 and 8.87).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example and evidence: tamarins were never exposed to the 'same' test pattern after habituation, so half the plotted data could not exist. This paper was retracted in 2010. The entry illustrates fabrication as publishing data that were never obtained or inventing subject counts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Falsified coding to produce statistical significance (unpublished experiments)
rubrics_metrics.description: In two unpublished experiments on tamarin responses to consonant-vowel strings, Respondent falsified the coding of some monkeys’ responses, making results statistically significant when the results coded by others were non-significant. Respondent acknowledged miscoding and that the study failed to support the hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrates falsification by altering/coding observational data to change statistical outcomes. These studies were not written up for publication; collaborators were informed and findings were corrected in internal records.

rubrics_metrics.name: False description of coding methodology and fabricated inter-observer reliabilities
rubrics_metrics.description: In versions of a manuscript ('Grammatical Pattern Learning by Human Infants and Monkeys') Respondent falsely described that 'two blind observers' coded trials (with a third to resolve differences) when in fact one experiment was coded only by the Respondent; later claimed 'Inter-observer reliabilities ranged from 0.85 to 0.90' although one experiment had only one observer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This criterion covers misrepresenting methods that affect validity (blinding, inter-rater reliability). The false methodological descriptions led to false proportions/numbers of animals showing favorable responses; collaborators recoded and corrected issues prior to final publication (Cognition 2007).

rubrics_metrics.name: False reporting of exact subject responses and sample counts
rubrics_metrics.description: In Hauser, M.D., Glynn, D., Wood, J. 'Rhesus monkeys correctly read the goal relevant gestures of a human agent.' Proc. R. Soc. B 274:1913-1918, 2007, Respondent reported 31/40 monkeys approached the target in one trial while records showed only 27/40; both results were statistically significant but the reported count was false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Misreporting numeric outcomes or sample counts is a form of falsification even if the overall statistical conclusion might remain significant; accurate reporting of raw counts is required for reproducibility and audit.

rubrics_metrics.name: False statement about videotaping / data archiving
rubrics_metrics.description: Respondent falsely claimed in the paper’s Materials and Methods that 'each trial was videotaped' when, for the 'Pointing without food' trials, there were only 30 videotapes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate statements about data collection/archiving (e.g., whether trials were videotaped) are required. Misstatements hinder verification and can mask data gaps. The authors later replicated findings with complete data and video records.

rubrics_metrics.name: False statement about subject identification leading to possible repeated testing
rubrics_metrics.description: In Wood, J.N., Glynn, D.D., Phillips, B.C., & Hauser, M.D. 'The perception of rational, goal-directed action in nonhuman primates.' Science 317:1402-1405, 2007, the supporting online material claimed 'All individuals are . . . readily identifiable by natural markings along with chest and leg tattoos and ear notches.' In fact only ~50% of subjects could be identified by these methods, allowing the possibility of repeated testing of the same animal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accurate reporting of subject identification procedures is necessary to prevent pseudoreplication and ensure validity of sample independence. This misstatement necessitated replication with complete datasets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inconsistent recoding that shifts results toward predicted hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: In an unpublished playback experiment with rhesus monkeys (AXA pattern), after initial coding by a research assistant and agreement that the original procedure was incorrect, the Respondent recoded 201 trials; his codes differed from the original in 36 cases, 29 in the theoretically predicted direction, producing p < 0.01. Respondent later acknowledged the coding was incorrect and the study failed to support the hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This documents the pattern of recoding or selectively changing codes to produce statistically significant results; such practice is falsification. It underscores the need for independent reliability checks and preservation of original coding records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative sanctions and restrictions on research/peer-review roles
rubrics_metrics.description: Hauser agreed to a three-year period (starting Aug 9, 2012) in which any of his research funded by the Public Health Service will be supervised and certified; he is barred from doing any peer review for the PHS and from serving on any PHS committees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sanctions are part of ORI outcomes: supervised research certification and exclusion from peer-review/committee service are remedies to limit future unsupervised influence on federally funded research. Note Respondent 'neither admits nor denies' misconduct yet accepts these administrative conditions; he had resigned from Harvard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction as corrective action for published misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cognition 2002 paper containing fabricated data was retracted in 2010.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction of affected publications is a standard corrective step where fabrication/falsification undermines the integrity of the published record.

rubrics_metrics.name: False or fraudulent statements in grant applications may have legal consequences
rubrics_metrics.description: Commentary on the page notes that submission of false data in a grant application is a federal crime punishable by imprisonment and/or fine (example cited: Eric Poehlman sentenced in 2006); making false statements on grant reports can be a felony (e.g., 18 U.S.C. §1001).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highlights that beyond institutional/administrative sanctions, falsifying grant data or progress reports can trigger criminal liability; it serves as a legal deterrent and a background standard for evaluating the severity of misconduct.
